summary.text: The Igala held the Niger–Benue confluence and the crossings of the lower Niger. Their armies fought on foot with spears, swords and bows, and crossed the Niger to invade Benin in 1515. The Attah also ruled through awe: he crowned rulers from Nsukka to the Niger.

arms.text: Spears, swords and bows were the arms of Igala armies before guns.
The Igala held the Niger crossings below the confluence; an army crossed the river to invade Benin.
Vassals and crowned rulers from Panda and Igu to the northern Igbo towns.
The Attah’s sacred kingship: rulers far beyond Idah sought his crown.
Guns came late, through the river trade of the 19th century.

record.text: The invasion of Benin came close to the city, and after two years the Igala forces were driven back across the Niger to Idah. Benin counts it a victory; in Igala memory it was no defeat, for Benin never crossed the river and Idah paid it no tribute.
Attah Ayegba refused the tribute; the Jukun army that came to enforce it was beaten, and Idah was free of Wukari.

record.against: Fulani-led Nupe armies of the jihad
record.text: Igala tradition tells of a victory at Igu (Koton Karfe) that stopped the jihad’s advance. With the Ebira and the Koto, the town was raided and burned more than once but never conquered, and in 1841 it still paid tribute to the Attah.
Nupe raids emptied Adda Kuddu in 1838 and broke the Attah’s hold on the north after 1853; Koton Karfe was raided but never conquered, and the heartland held.
